item.research_question: How does the phase structure (single-phase vs. multiphase) of Al_x CoCrFeNi high entropy alloys influence their precipitation behavior and structural stability under ion irradiation?
item.processing_route: Arc-melting pure metals (purity >99.6 wt.%) in Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere, remelted at least four times, drop-cast into mold, cut into 1 mm thick pieces, polished, and prepared as TEM foils via dual jet polishing in ethanol with 5% HClO4
item.test_conditions: Ion irradiation with 3 MeV Au ions at room temperature, fluences ranging from 1 × 10^14 to 1 × 10^16 cm^-2, ion flux ~3 × 10^11 cm^-2 s^-1, corresponding to up to ~43 dpa within 100 nm depth
key_findings: The single-phase Al_0.1 CoCrFeNi alloy exhibited no precipitates even at the highest fluence of 1 × 10^16 cm^-2 (~43 dpa).
Numerous coherent nano-scale precipitates were observed in both multiphase alloys (x = 0.75 and 1.5) after irradiation.
Precipitates in the A2 phases of Al_1.5 CoCrFeNi showed the largest average size and distinct growth with increasing fluence due to coalescence.
Precipitates in the B2 phases of multiphase alloys were smaller and approached a saturation value with increasing fluence.
Precipitates in the fcc and A2 phases were enriched in Fe and Cr, while precipitates in the Al/Ni-enriched B2 phases were enriched in Co.
The average precipitate sizes in Cr/Fe-enriched fcc and A2 phases were obviously larger than those in the Al/Ni-enriched B2 phases for both multiphase HEAs.
No significant variation in SAED patterns or chemical compositions of different phases was found between virgin and as-irradiated samples, except for the new precipitates.
item.mechanism: The stability of the single-phase HEA is attributed to high configurational entropy reducing the thermodynamic driving force for precipitation and low atomic mobility (sluggish diffusion) kinetically restraining precipitate formation. In multiphase HEAs, phase separation and ordered phases reduce configurational entropy, causing them to behave like conventional binary/ternary alloys where positive mixing enthalpies (e.g., Fe-Cr) or negative enthalpies (e.g., Ni-Al) drive precipitation under irradiation-induced defect fluxes.
item.limitations: Quantitative chemical analysis of precipitates via EELS and nano-EDX has large errors because precipitate sizes are much smaller than the TEM sample thickness; irradiation responses at high temperatures were not studied as the experiments were conducted at room temperature.
item.future_work: Further systematic studies on the irradiation responses of HEAs at elevated temperatures are required for their applications in advanced nuclear systems.
quotes: No precipitate is observed even at the highest fluence.
The excellent structural stability against precipitation of Al 0.1 CoCrFeNi is attributed to the high configurational entropy and low atomic diffusion.

For the multiphase HEAs, the phase separations and formation of ordered phases reduce the system configurational entropy, resulting in the similar precipitation behavior with corresponding binary or ternary conventional alloys.
